Roth vs. traditional rollover: what happens when you convert a 401(k) or TSP

A traditional-to-traditional rollover moves pre-tax money from a 401(k) or TSP into an IRA with no tax due now. A Roth conversion moves the same money into a Roth account, so the converted amount is taxed as income this year, cannot be undone, and no longer has required withdrawals during your lifetime.

By Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent (NPN 21370662) · November 2026

Rollover paperwork usually offers two boxes: traditional IRA, or Roth. One keeps the tax bill where it was; the other brings it forward to this year. This guide uses the IRS's published pages on rollovers, IRAs and conversions and designated Roth accounts. It is general information, not tax advice.

Three moves that look alike but tax differently

  • Traditional 401(k) or TSP to a traditional IRA. Pre-tax money stays pre-tax. Done as a direct rollover, nothing is taxed and nothing is withheld now. You pay income tax later, when you withdraw.
  • Traditional 401(k) or TSP to a Roth IRA (a conversion). The IRS puts it plainly: a conversion to a Roth IRA "results in taxation of any untaxed amounts." The whole pre-tax balance you convert, including earnings, is added to your income for the year.
  • Roth 401(k) or Roth TSP to a Roth IRA. Already-taxed Roth money moves to a Roth IRA with no new tax. The IRS notes that designated Roth money may roll to another designated Roth account or a Roth IRA, but not to a traditional IRA.

Many plans also allow an in-plan Roth rollover, where pre-tax money is converted to the Roth side of the same 401(k). The IRS says this "usually results in taxable income to the participant" and "cannot be reversed after the transfer is made."

What a conversion does to this year's tax bill

The converted amount is taxed as ordinary income in the year of the conversion, on top of your wages, pension, Social Security and any other income. A large conversion can push part of your income into a higher bracket, and it raises the income figure that other income-based rules key off. That is why many people convert in pieces over several years, and why the year matters as much as the amount.

Two practical points from the IRS rollover rules apply here. First, if the plan pays the money to you instead of sending it directly to the new account, the plan must withhold 20% for federal tax "even if you intend to roll it over later." A direct, account-to-account conversion avoids that. Second, the once-per-year limit on IRA rollovers does not apply to conversions or to trustee-to-trustee transfers.

Plan to pay the tax from other money
  • If you hold back part of the converted balance to cover the tax, the part held back is a distribution: it is taxed, it does not land in the Roth, and if you are under 59½ a 10% additional tax may apply.
  • The TSP says the same thing about its in-plan conversions: you "cannot use part of the amount you're converting to pay taxes."
  • Estimated tax or extra withholding on other income may be needed so you are not short in April.

Why you cannot change your mind

Until 2017 a conversion could be "recharacterized," meaning undone, if the market fell or the tax bill turned out larger than expected. That door is closed. The IRS states that a conversion made on or after January 1, 2018 cannot be recharacterized, and the same prohibition covers amounts rolled to a Roth IRA from an employer plan. In-plan conversions and TSP conversions are also final once processed.

The required-withdrawal trade

The upside of paying tax now is what happens later. The IRS says you generally have to start taking required minimum distributions from traditional IRAs and workplace plans at age 73. You are not required to take withdrawals from a Roth IRA, or from a designated Roth account in a 401(k) or 403(b), during your lifetime. Beneficiaries still have withdrawal rules, so a conversion changes the timing of the tax, not whether the account eventually pays out. Qualified Roth withdrawals are generally not taxed; read the holding-period rules on the IRS pages above before you count on them.

Deciding between a rollover and a conversion?

We will walk through the two paths, what each does to your taxes and your required withdrawals, and what to ask your plan and your tax preparer. No pressure.

TSP: the in-plan conversion option

Since January 28, 2026, the TSP offers a Roth in-plan conversion inside My Account. The TSP's own announcement lists the conditions: the conversion amount "becomes part of your taxable income for the year," the tax must be paid "using personal funds from another source," and "once you do a conversion, you cannot reverse it or change it." The TSP recommends talking with a tax advisor first. If you would rather move TSP money out, see our TSP rollover guide.

Who tends to convert, and who tends to wait

  • A conversion often gets a closer look in a year when income is lower than usual (a gap year between work and Social Security, for example), when a pre-tax balance is large enough that required withdrawals at 73 would be unwelcome, or when heirs are expected to be in higher brackets than the account owner.
  • A traditional rollover often wins when this year's bracket is already high, when the money may be needed within a few years, when there is no outside cash to pay the tax, or when state income tax on the conversion would be heavy.
  • Age matters. The 20% withholding, the 10% additional tax under 59½ on any amount not rolled over, and the age-73 withdrawal rules all change the math at different ages.

Income limits do not decide this for you. The IRS limits who may contribute to a Roth IRA (for 2026 the phase-out is $153,000 to $168,000 single and $242,000 to $252,000 married filing jointly, per IRS Notice 2025-67), but there is no income limit on conversions, and the IRS says the contribution limit "does not apply to rollover contributions."

Roth money and annuities

If the destination is an annuity rather than a mutual fund IRA, the same traditional-or-Roth question applies, and the conversion tax is the same. Annuities are insurance contracts, not investments in the stock market; they may carry surrender charges and fees, and guarantees depend on the issuing company's claims-paying ability. See Roth IRA and Roth 401(k) rollovers to an annuity and our annuities page.

In your state

The conversion tax rules above are federal. State income tax on a conversion, and the insurance products available to receive the money, vary by state. Common questions

Roth conversion FAQ

Is there an income limit on a Roth conversion?
No. The IRS income limits apply to Roth IRA contributions, not to conversions. Anyone with a traditional 401(k), TSP or IRA balance can generally convert, but the converted amount is taxed as income in that year. The IRS FAQ on IRAs and the designated Roth account page explain the rules.
Does a conversion count against my yearly contribution limit?
No. The IRS says the IRA contribution limit does not apply to rollover contributions, and a conversion is treated as a rollover for that purpose. The 2026 limits of $7,500 for an IRA and $24,500 for a 401(k) or TSP are separate from any amount you convert.
Can I convert my TSP to Roth without leaving federal service?
Yes, since January 28, 2026 the TSP offers a Roth in-plan conversion inside My Account for traditional (pre-tax) balances. The converted amount is taxable income for the year, you must pay the tax from other money, and the conversion cannot be reversed. Read the TSP announcement and talk with a tax advisor first.
